planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Viognier is a moderately vigorous variety that can struggle with poor, uneven fruit set in unfavorable spring weather.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Viognier is a white wine grape native to the Rhône Valley of France, historically centered on the tiny appellation of Condrieu, where it came perilously close to disappearing entirely in the mid-20th century before a revival brought it back to prominence in France, California, and beyond. The grape produces full-bodied, richly aromatic white wines with pronounced notes of peach, apricot, and honeysuckle, a distinctive perfumed character that sets it apart from crisper, more neutral white varieties. The vine can be inconsistent in fruit set, sometimes producing loose, uneven clusters in cool or wet spring weather, so site selection and bloom-time weather matter more for Viognier than for many other varieties. Train to a permanent trellis, thin fruit if clusters set unevenly, and pick based on aromatic ripeness, since Viognier can lose its signature perfume if left to hang too long.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; the notably thick skin of Petite Sirah gives it above-average resistance to bunch rot in humid conditions compared with thinner-skinned varieties.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Petite Sirah, more accurately known by its French name Durif after the botanist who discovered it as a chance cross of Syrah and the obscure Peloursin grape in the 1800s, produces small, thick-skinned, intensely dark berries despite the confusingly similar name to Syrah, which it is genetically related to but distinct from. Wines are deeply colored, high in tannin, and robust, often used both as a standalone bold red and as a blending grape to add color, structure, and backbone to lighter varieties. The unusually thick skin gives the variety real practical resilience against bunch rot and splitting in humid or rainy conditions, an advantage over many thinner-skinned fine wine grapes. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the naturally vigorous canopy for airflow, and pick once tannins are ripe as well as sugars, since underripe Petite Sirah can taste harshly astringent.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Cabernet Franc buds and ripens earlier and tolerates cold better than Cabernet Sauvignon, giving it a wider climate range.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Cabernet Franc is a red Bordeaux grape historically important as one of the two parent varieties of Cabernet Sauvignon (along with Sauvignon Blanc), and it remains widely grown both as a blending grape and as a distinctive varietal wine in its own right, particularly in the Loire Valley of France. Wines are generally lighter in body and tannin than Cabernet Sauvignon, with a distinctive aromatic profile often described as bell pepper, violet, and red berry, and the grape's earlier ripening window and better cold tolerance make it more reliably productive than Cabernet Sauvignon in cooler or shorter-season growing regions. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for good sun exposure on developing clusters to soften the variety's herbaceous, green-pepper character, and harvest once tannins are fully ripe rather than relying on sugar level alone.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sémillon's thin skin makes it susceptible to noble rot (Botrytis cinerea) under humid autumn conditions, a trait deliberately exploited for sweet wine production but a liability where dry table wine is the goal.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Sémillon is a Bordeaux white wine grape best known as the primary variety behind the legendary sweet dessert wines of Sauternes, where its thin skin readily allows infection by Botrytis cinerea, the 'noble rot' fungus that concentrates sugars and adds distinctive honeyed, apricot flavors to the shriveled berries; the same grape also makes excellent dry white wine, often blended with Sauvignon Blanc, with a rounder, waxier, honeyed character. Because the thin skin that enables noble rot production is a liability for growers aiming to make dry wine in humid climates, site selection and vineyard management differ significantly depending on the intended wine style. Train to a permanent trellis, and decide harvest timing based on style: pick at standard ripeness for dry wine, or allow extended hang time under the right humid autumn conditions if noble rot development is the goal.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Barbera is a vigorous, adaptable, productive vine that performs reliably across a fairly wide range of climates.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Barbera is a red wine grape native to the Piedmont region of northern Italy, historically the everyday table wine of the region before a wave of quality-focused winemaking in the late 20th century elevated it to serious status, prized for naturally high acidity paired with relatively low tannin, producing fresh, juicy, food-friendly red wines with bright cherry and berry flavors. The vine is notably vigorous and productive, more forgiving and adaptable to a range of growing conditions than many of the finicky, low-yielding grapes used for premium wine, which has made it a popular choice both in its native Italy and increasingly in New World regions including California. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor and crop load through canopy work and thinning to avoid diluted flavor from overcropping, and harvest once sugars are adequate, since Barbera's naturally high acidity gives some flexibility in exact picking date.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
